messages.subject: Re: Bootstrapped confidence intervals for standardized parameters
messages.subject_clean: Bootstrapped confidence intervals for standardized parameters
messages.body_plain:
If you *really* want to do this, then *technically* there are several ways. Assuming you don't want to omit the acceleration procedure (bca.simple is actually bc), you can use the boot package among others. Here is a very simple example (note: no error handler and so on):

library(lavaan)
library(boot)

model <<- '
  # Simplified example
  ind60 =~ x1 + x2 + x3
  dem60 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4
  dem60 ~ b * ind60
'

# Function to obtain standardized value for b
param <- function(d, i) {
  fit <- sem(model, data = d[i,])
  pe <- parameterEstimates(fit, standardized = TRUE)
  return(
    pe[pe$label == "b",]$std.all
  )
}

# Bootstrap
res <- boot(data = PoliticalDemocracy, statistic = param, R = 1000)
print(res)

# 95% CI
boot.ci <http://boot.ci>(res, type="bca", conf = 0.95, index = 1)

messages.subject: Re: Trying to estimate the stability of a variable using Lavaan.
messages.subject_clean: Trying to estimate the stability of a variable using Lavaan.
messages.body_plain:
Lucas

This model is not evluating stability over time

mod <- "
  x =~ t1 + t2 + t3
"

This model would be testing is the three time pints consistently measure a single underlying construct X

Doing dybamic models is not straightforward in lavaan. You can only estimate them with some data managemet includedm for example with Latent Differntial Equation (LDE) with time delay embedding matrices, or estimated derivatives

Meaning the cross-lag model that you could estimate with lavaan is not a dynamic model, but a discrete time cross-lag model. The closest you could do is a latent growth curve model (which is a continuous time model), or latent change score model (simplest form of differential models).

a) If you were to estimate the cross-lag panel model, you could create a phantom factor at each time point and evaluate the stability/auto-regression between time points (lag-dependent)
b) You could also evaluate the mean differences over time with latent change score models
c) estimate a latent growth curve, estimating mean difference over time, and the variability across subjetcs
d) if you want to do dynamic models I would recommend you the ctsem or dynr R packages, which do dynamic SEM models. ctsem do dynamic continuous time models from the Exact Discrete Model approach. And dynr do dynamic continuous and discrete time models from the state space model approach

Not sure how far you have gone through the dynamic modeling literature, because I am throwing a lot of terminaology here. In case some relevant terms
- dynamic modelling
- continuous time models
- discrete time models

Depending on which approach you use, the term "stability" can mean different things. Could you explan more what do you mean by it?

Here are some useful references

Bertenthal, B. I. (2007). Dynamical Systems: It is about time! In S. M. Boker & M. J. Wenger (Eds.), Data Analytic Techniques for Dynamical Systems. Lawrence Erlbaum Associates, Inc.

messages.subject: Re: Bootstrapped confidence intervals for standardized parameters
messages.subject_clean: Bootstrapped confidence intervals for standardized parameters
messages.body_plain:
You can do this step by step, but you don't have to. Here is a simple example with several coefficients (it also works with latent variables):

library(lavaan)
library(boot)

# Some data
set.seed(1234)
X <- rnorm(1000)
M <- 0.3 * X + rnorm(1000)
Y <- 0.4 * M + rnorm(1000)
myData <- data.frame(X = X, Y = Y, M = M)

# Simple mediation model
myModel <- '
M ~ a * X
Y ~ b * M + c * X
ind := a * b
'

# Function to obtain standardized values
param <- function(d, i) {
  fit <- sem(myModel, data = d[i,])

  pe <- parameterEstimates(fit, standardized = TRUE)
  return(

    c(
      pe[pe$label == "a",]$std.all,
      pe[pe$label == "b",]$std.all,
      pe[pe$label == "c",]$std.all,
      pe[pe$label == "ind",]$std.all
    )
  )
}

# Bootstrap
res <- boot(data = myData, statistic = param, R = 1000)

print(res)

# 95% CI
boot.ci <http://boot.ci>(res, type="bca", conf = 0.95, index = 1)

boot.ci <http://boot.ci>(res, type="bca", conf = 0.95, index = 2)
boot.ci <http://boot.ci>(res, type="bca", conf = 0.95, index = 3)
boot.ci <http://boot.ci>(res, type="bca", conf = 0.95, index = 4)

Note: I only want to show how you can solve the problem "technically". This is not a statement about the usefulness of these confidence intervals.

Model1 <- 'V1 =~ Va + Vb + Vc
                   V1 ~ X1 + X2 + X3'

Model 1<- 'V1 =~ Va + Vb + Vc
                    V1 <~ X1 + X2 + X3'

2. Where can I find information or examples of MIMIC modesl utilizing Lavaan? I really cannot seem to find much information on MIMIC models with Lavaan.

Thanks!
Jessica

messages.body_plain:
Dear Mauricio,

Thank you very much for such a thorough answer.

Here's what I mean by stability of a variable: suppose I'm interested in measuring a construct such as ideology and that, in a panel survey, we ask participants about where they are placed in the ideological spectrum at T1, T2, and T3. Now, if we observe changes in that variable over time, we cannot be sure that this variation is driven by respondents truly changing their ideological self-placement or if it's driven by measurement error. So, basically, I want to distinguish true changes in a variable from measurement error.

Here are some papers that do exactly what I want to do:
Using dynamic panels – Schickler, E., & Green, D. P. (1997). The stability of party identification in western democracies: results from eight panel surveys. Comparative Political Studies, 30(4), 450-483. https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0010414097030004003
Using SEM – Prior, M. (2010). You’ve either got it or you don’t? The stability of political interest over the life cycle. The Journal of Politics, 72(3), 747-766. https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/full/10.1017/S0022381610000149?casa_token=XTEnDq0JMZgAAAAA%3APwwMXoMYu4SmFQCyaI0XySJLDucT9F7jsC3ALjyugW7-eIa8vIOw4mBN4uDi9NXcnjBh8S6J2HKG
Using SEM – Tucker, P. D., Montgomery, J. M., & Smith, S. S. (2019). Party Identification in the Age of Obama: Evidence on the Sources of Stability and Systematic Change in Party Identification from a Long-Term Panel Survey. Political Research Quarterly, 72(2), 309-328. https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/1065912918784215
Using SEM (and Lavaan, for that matter) – Kustov, A., Laaker, D., & Reller, C. (2019). The stability of immigration attitudes: Evidence and implications. Available at SSRN 3322121. https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3322121

According to your description, it seems that a) is closer to what I want, correct? Any suggestion as to how to implement it in the simple context I described in my first email?

Thanks, again,

-- Lucas de Abreu Maia, he/him/his
Ph.D. candidate | Department of Political Science | University of California, San Diego

messages.body_plain:
Re (1) This is hardly surprising. Look at the df of the two models.  Model1 has 6 df and Model2 7 df. If you now examine the parameter tables, you will see that V1 ~~ V1 is not freely estimated for Model2. If you add V1 ~~ V1 to this model, you will get the same results as with Model1.

Here is a sample code to show this:

library(lavaan)

# Some strange data
set.seed(1234)
Va <- rnorm(1000)
Vb <- 0.9 * Va + rnorm(1000)
Vc <- 0.9 * Va + rnorm(1000)
X1 <- 0.2 * Va + rnorm(1000)
X2 <- 0.3 * Va + rnorm(1000)
X3 <- 0.4 * Va + rnorm(1000)
myData <- data.frame(Va = Va, Vb = Vb, Vc = Vc, X1 = X1, X2 = X2, X3 = X3)

myModel1 ='

V1 =~ Va + Vb + Vc
V1 ~ X1 + X2 + X3'

myModel2 ='

V1 =~ Va + Vb + Vc
V1 <~ X1 + X2 + X3'

fit1 <- sem(myModel1, myData)
fit2 <- sem(myModel2, myData)

fitMeasures(fit1, c("chisq", "df"))
fitMeasures(fit2, c("chisq", "df"))

parameterTable(fit1)
parameterTable(fit2)

myModel3 ='

V1 =~ Va + Vb + Vc
V1 <~ X1 + X2 + X3

V1 ~~ V1'

fit3 <- sem(myModel3, myData)

fitMeasures(fit3, c("chisq", "df"))

I see no reason to fix V1 =~ Va and V1 ~~ V1 (Model2 without modification).

messages.body_plain:
Lucas

General comments, if you have one 1 indicator per time point the separation of real change and measurement error is limited. If you only have 3 time points, will limit the models you can estimate. Are your indicators continuous, or categorical? There seems to be variation in these papers on how the type of indicators and how to treat them. The models I suggested only applied for continuous indicators

After a quick look at some of these papers, they treat the topic of stability in very different ways. Kustov, A., Laaker, D., & Reller, C. (2019) seems to do the auto-regressive models,  Schickler, E., & Green, D. P. (1997) seems to be doing a model when they treat the indicators as dichotomous, and Tucker, P. D., Montgomery, J. M., & Smith, S. S. (2019) do an extension of the latent growth curve model.

So,  I am not clear how you want to measure this "stability", also of your indicator is categorical, then I dont think these models would be recommended. But would suggest a Markov Model for change of category over time

I can show you syntax for some of these models, but dont want to show you syntax for a wrong model

When you say " simple context I described in my first email? ", sadly a simple contaxt doesnt provide me with enough information about what is the data like (continuous/categorical) and what is the model?

messages.body_plain:
I'll chime in that change in the sense of stability can be relative (position in the cohort) or absolute  (position on the scale) and these have historically often been conflated under the same label.

The autoregressive approach assesses relative stability: if the entire cohort increases by the same amount due to secular trends or some external event, that's highly stable in the relative sense even if the numbers change.

The latent growth/trajectory approach better gets at absolute stability (i.e., on the time-1 metric) by looking at both mean and variance in change over time. You'd want to see very small mean and variance of the slope to conclude absolute stability.

Pat

>
> So,  I am not clear how you want to measure this "stability", also of your indicator is categorical, then I dont think these models would be recommended. But would suggest a Markov Model for change of category over time

messages.subject_clean: Bootstrapped confidence intervals for standardized parameters
messages.body_plain:
Thank you so much,
Your example works.
I am new to SEM. So,  I do not really know whether CI for standardized coefficients are useful. In my field (environmental conservation), SEM is not much used and people like to see p-values or CI, so that is why I wanted to do it.
But, would you let me know why CI for standardized coefficients may not be useful?
Thank you,

On Monday, January 4, 2021 at 6:54:02 AM UTC-5 car...@web.de wrote:
> You can do this step by step, but you don't have to. Here is a simple example with several coefficients (it also works with latent variables):
>
> library(lavaan)
> library(boot)
>
> # Some data
> set.seed(1234)
> X <- rnorm(1000)
> M <- 0.3 * X + rnorm(1000)
> Y <- 0.4 * M + rnorm(1000)
> myData <- data.frame(X = X, Y = Y, M = M)
>
> # Simple mediation model
> myModel <- '
> M ~ a * X
> Y ~ b * M + c * X
> ind := a * b
> '
>
> # Function to obtain standardized values
> param <- function(d, i) {
>   fit <- sem(myModel, data = d[i,])
>
>   pe <- parameterEstimates(fit, standardized = TRUE)
>   return(
>     c(
>       pe[pe$label == "a",]$std.all,
>       pe[pe$label == "b",]$std.all,
>       pe[pe$label == "c",]$std.all,
>       pe[pe$label == "ind",]$std.all
>     )
>   )
> }
>
>
> # Bootstrap
> res <- boot(data = myData, statistic = param, R = 1000)
>
> print(res)
>
> # 95% CI
> boot.ci <http://boot.ci>(res, type="bca", conf = 0.95, index = 1)
> boot.ci <http://boot.ci>(res, type="bca", conf = 0.95, index = 2)
> boot.ci <http://boot.ci>(res, type="bca", conf = 0.95, index = 3)
> boot.ci <http://boot.ci>(res, type="bca", conf = 0.95, index = 4)
>
>
> Note: I only want to show how you can solve the problem "technically". This is not a statement about the usefulness of these confidence intervals.
>
>
>

> > In the example you provided there is only one standardized coefficient. How to do it with multiple coefficients? Or should I do it one by one?

messages.body_plain:
I explicitly did not write a statement about the usefulness of these confidence intervals. On the one hand, inferences (hypothesis testing) should be based on unstandardized parameters. On the other hand, CI around standardized coefficients may be understood as a quantification of uncertainty. In a slightly different context, you can find some statements here: https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/OfaPfUYqVVI/m/ZXzk3f0aDQAJ

messages.body_plain:
Hi, Mauricio:

Again, thanks for helping with this and engaging with my question. You're being very generous with your time.

The variable I'm analyzing is continuous.

Sorry, I directed you to the wrong work by Green and Schickler. I actually meant to refer to their book Partisan Hearts and Minds: https://books.google.com/books?hl=en&lr=&id=HVY18n59ThgC&oi=fnd&pg=PP9&dq=schickler+and+green+stability+partisanship&ots=cMtmaXUxmx&sig=0ydUnOXV4mfHfgEMHSSUZERdJV8#v=onepage&q=schickler%20and%20green%20stability%20partisanship&f=false. They implement an autoregressor model on a continuous variable (chapter 3). But they don't use SEM at all. They employ the Anderson and Hsiao (1981) and Arellano (1989) estimators. It's a little outdated, so that's why I wanted to implement a measurement model, as used by the more recent papers I cited in the previous email.

So, to summarize, the autoregressor model is really what I'm looking for. I understand that a three-wave panel may be too short for me to draw inferences from, but, in actuality, I'm analyzing a bunch of different panels, some of them with many more waves. I'm just starting from the simplest possible case. After that, I should be able to expand the code myself to panels with additional waves.

So, to recap, here's the data I have: a three-wave panel in which I'm interested in a continuous variable. I want to use an autoregressor model to get at how much this variable changes over time. Does that make sense?

Best wishes and thanks, again,

-- Lucas de Abreu Maia, he/him/his
Ph.D. candidate | Department of Political Science | University of California, San Diego
lucasamaia.com <http://lucasamaia.com/>

messages.body_plain:
Lucas

Ok, an autoregressor model with SEM could be done in a couple of different ways.

1. You maintain the metric and scale for the the original variable scales. This one could be done directly using the variables. With a lag 1 regression between them, we are labeling this AR1 regression a1 so that we are stating that stability effect is the same between time points
mod_reg1 <- '
t3 ~ a1*t2
t2 ~ a1*t1
'

2. You standardized the variables at each time point by creating phantom factors, and express the variance differences in the factor loadings, and mean differences in the indicator means
mod_reg2 <- '
#### phantom variables
## estimate factor loadings: standard deviations at each time point
ph_t1 =~ NA*t1
ph_t2 =~ NA*t2
ph_t3 =~ NA*t3
## fix factor variances at 1
ph_t1 ~~ 1*ph_t1
ph_t2 ~~ 1*ph_t2
ph_t3 ~~ 1*ph_t3
## fix factor means at 0
ph_t1 ~0*1
ph_t2 ~0*1
ph_t3 ~0*1
## fix indicator variances at 0. Meaning all the variance falls into the factor
t1 ~~ 0*t1
t2 ~~ 0*t2
t3 ~~ 0*t3
#### aut regression
ph_t3 ~  a1*ph_t2
ph_t2 ~  a1* ph_t1
'

3. The third options I would recommend is to use ctsem for continuous time panel models (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ctsem/index.html)

The disadvantge of 1 and 2 is that they are lag dependent, meaning that you are only presenting the auto-effect for the respective lag of time between your measurements. Option 3 allows to estimate the auto-effect independent of lag and evaluate the effect at different lags.
For example, 2 can be seen as an AR1, withount mean differences, while 1 would be cluser to ARM1, which allows for mean changes over time

I think something like this is what you are looking for?

On Mon, Jan 4, 2021 at 4:40 PM Mauricio Garnier-Villarreal <mauga...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Lucas
>
> Ok, an autoregressor model with SEM could be done in a couple of different ways.
>
> 1. You maintain the metric and scale for the the original variable scales. This one could be done directly using the variables. With a lag 1 regression between them, we are labeling this AR1 regression a1 so that we are stating that stability effect is the same between time points
> mod_reg1 <- '
> t3 ~ a1*t2
> t2 ~ a1*t1
> '
>
> 2. You standardized the variables at each time point by creating phantom factors, and express the variance differences in the factor loadings, and mean differences in the indicator means
> mod_reg2 <- '
> #### phantom variables
> ## estimate factor loadings: standard deviations at each time point
> ph_t1 =~ NA*t1
> ph_t2 =~ NA*t2
> ph_t3 =~ NA*t3
> ## fix factor variances at 1
> ph_t1 ~~ 1*ph_t1
> ph_t2 ~~ 1*ph_t2
> ph_t3 ~~ 1*ph_t3
> ## fix factor means at 0
> ph_t1 ~0*1
> ph_t2 ~0*1
> ph_t3 ~0*1
> ## fix indicator variances at 0. Meaning all the variance falls into the factor
> t1 ~~ 0*t1
> t2 ~~ 0*t2
> t3 ~~ 0*t3
> #### aut regression
> ph_t3 ~  a1*ph_t2
> ph_t2 ~  a1* ph_t1
> '
>
> 3. The third options I would recommend is to use ctsem for continuous time panel models (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ctsem/index.html <https://urldefense.com/v3/__https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ctsem/index.html__;!!Mih3wA!XXrXPpm22V_0aDy8V3qTtHMfImn_ki7y-nOvsCtC-mKr6vyThAHDV2j3M8mSygdn$>)
>
>
> The disadvantge of 1 and 2 is that they are lag dependent, meaning that you are only presenting the auto-effect for the respective lag of time between your measurements. Option 3 allows to estimate the auto-effect independent of lag and evaluate the effect at different lags.
> For example, 2 can be seen as an AR1, withount mean differences, while 1 would be cluser to ARM1, which allows for mean changes over time
>
> I think something like this is what you are looking for?

> > Lucas
> >
> > Ok, an autoregressor model with SEM could be done in a couple of different ways.
> >
> > 1. You maintain the metric and scale for the the original variable scales. This one could be done directly using the variables. With a lag 1 regression between them, we are labeling this AR1 regression a1 so that we are stating that stability effect is the same between time points
> > mod_reg1 <- '
> > t3 ~ a1*t2
> > t2 ~ a1*t1
> > '
> >
> > 2. You standardized the variables at each time point by creating phantom factors, and express the variance differences in the factor loadings, and mean differences in the indicator means
> > mod_reg2 <- '
> > #### phantom variables
> > ## estimate factor loadings: standard deviations at each time point
> > ph_t1 =~ NA*t1
> > ph_t2 =~ NA*t2
> > ph_t3 =~ NA*t3
> > ## fix factor variances at 1
> > ph_t1 ~~ 1*ph_t1
> > ph_t2 ~~ 1*ph_t2
> > ph_t3 ~~ 1*ph_t3
> > ## fix factor means at 0
> > ph_t1 ~0*1
> > ph_t2 ~0*1
> > ph_t3 ~0*1
> > ## fix indicator variances at 0. Meaning all the variance falls into the factor
> > t1 ~~ 0*t1
> > t2 ~~ 0*t2
> > t3 ~~ 0*t3
> > #### aut regression
> > ph_t3 ~  a1*ph_t2
> > ph_t2 ~  a1* ph_t1
> > '
> >
> > 3. The third options I would recommend is to use ctsem for continuous time panel models (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ctsem/index.html <https://urldefense.com/v3/__https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ctsem/index.html__;!!Mih3wA!XXrXPpm22V_0aDy8V3qTtHMfImn_ki7y-nOvsCtC-mKr6vyThAHDV2j3M8mSygdn$>)
> >
> >
> > The disadvantge of 1 and 2 is that they are lag dependent, meaning that you are only presenting the auto-effect for the respective lag of time between your measurements. Option 3 allows to estimate the auto-effect independent of lag and evaluate the effect at different lags.
> > For example, 2 can be seen as an AR1, withount mean differences, while 1 would be cluser to ARM1, which allows for mean changes over time
> >
> > I think something like this is what you are looking for?

On Monday, January 4, 2021 at 3:46:18 PM UTC-5 car...@web.de wrote:
> I explicitly did not write a statement about the usefulness of these confidence intervals. On the one hand, inferences (hypothesis testing) should be based on unstandardized parameters. On the other hand, CI around standardized coefficients may be understood as a quantification of uncertainty. In a slightly different context, you can find some statements here: https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/OfaPfUYqVVI/m/ZXzk3f0aDQAJ
> Am 04.01.21, 18:11 schrieb "rras...@gmail.com" <rras...@gmail.com>:
> > Thank you so much,
> > Your example works.
> > I am new to SEM. So,  I do not really know whether CI for standardized coefficients are useful. In my field (environmental conservation), SEM is not much used and people like to see p-values or CI, so that is why I wanted to do it.
> > But, would you let me know why CI for standardized coefficients may not be useful?
> > Thank you,
> >
> >
> > On Monday, January 4, 2021 at 6:54:02 AM UTC-5 car...@web.de wrote:
> > > You can do this step by step, but you don't have to. Here is a simple example with several coefficients (it also works with latent variables):
> > >
> > > library(lavaan)
> > > library(boot)
> > >
> > > # Some data
> > > set.seed(1234)
> > > X <- rnorm(1000)
> > > M <- 0.3 * X + rnorm(1000)
> > > Y <- 0.4 * M + rnorm(1000)
> > > myData <- data.frame(X = X, Y = Y, M = M)
> > >
> > > # Simple mediation model
> > > myModel <- '
> > > M ~ a * X
> > > Y ~ b * M + c * X
> > > ind := a * b
> > > '
> > >
> > > # Function to obtain standardized values
> > > param <- function(d, i) {
> > >   fit <- sem(myModel, data = d[i,])
> > >
> > >   pe <- parameterEstimates(fit, standardized = TRUE)
> > >   return(
> > >     c(
> > >       pe[pe$label == "a",]$std.all,
> > >       pe[pe$label == "b",]$std.all,
> > >       pe[pe$label == "c",]$std.all,
> > >       pe[pe$label == "ind",]$std.all
> > >     )
> > >   )
> > > }
> > >
> > >
> > > # Bootstrap
> > > res <- boot(data = myData, statistic = param, R = 1000)
> > >
> > > print(res)
> > >
> > > # 95% CI
> > > boot.ci <http://boot.ci>(res, type="bca", conf = 0.95, index = 1)
> > > boot.ci <http://boot.ci>(res, type="bca", conf = 0.95, index = 2)
> > > boot.ci <http://boot.ci>(res, type="bca", conf = 0.95, index = 3)
> > > boot.ci <http://boot.ci>(res, type="bca", conf = 0.95, index = 4)
> > >
> > >
> > > Note: I only want to show how you can solve the problem "technically". This is not a statement about the usefulness of these confidence intervals.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > Am 04.01.2021 um 03:17 schrieb rras...@gmail.com:
> > > > Thank you so much!
> > > > In the example you provided there is only one standardized coefficient. How to do it with multiple coefficients? Or should I do it one by one?

messages.subject_clean: MIMIC model proper syntax?
messages.body_plain:
The syntax is irrelevant for lavaan (myModel2 and myModel3 are identical). The syntax that is easier to read for humans should be preferred. If you are looking for some kind of standard, keep in mind that the label "V1" does not really signal that V1 is a factor. Detached from this, you could also think about this version:

myModel4 ='

V1 =~ Va + Vb + Vc
V1 <~ X1 + X2 + X3'

fit4 <- sem(myModel4, myData, std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE)

Now identification is achieved via std.lv <http://std.lv> (V1 ~~  V1 fixed) and V1 =~ Va is freely estimated.

messages.body_plain:
Thanks, Mauricio. The code worked beautifully. Actually, I ran your first two suggestions and they spelled out similar results. I just want to make sure that I'm interpreting the results (passed below) correctly; do they indicate that the average result of the time trends is approximately 0.6 and that the effect is distinguishable from 0–i.e., that the variable is not very stable over time?

Code (d is the dataset and I'm using Huber-White robust SEs):
> mod_reg1 <- '
+   t3 ~ a1*t2
+   t2 ~ a1*t1
+ '
>
> fit1 <- sem(mod_reg1, d,
+   orthogonal = T, se="robust.huber.white")
> summary(fit1)

> > > mod_reg1 <- '
> > > t3 ~ a1*t2

> > > '
> > >
> > > 2. You standardized the variables at each time point by creating phantom factors, and express the variance differences in the factor loadings, and mean differences in the indicator means

> > > ## estimate factor loadings: standard deviations at each time point
> > > ph_t1 =~ NA*t1
> > > ph_t2 =~ NA*t2
> > > ph_t3 =~ NA*t3
> > > ## fix factor variances at 1
> > > ph_t1 ~~ 1*ph_t1
> > > ph_t2 ~~ 1*ph_t2
> > > ph_t3 ~~ 1*ph_t3
> > > ## fix factor means at 0
> > > ph_t1 ~0*1
> > > ph_t2 ~0*1
> > > ph_t3 ~0*1
> > > ## fix indicator variances at 0. Meaning all the variance falls into the factor
> > > t1 ~~ 0*t1
> > > t2 ~~ 0*t2
> > > t3 ~~ 0*t3
> > > #### aut regression
> > > ph_t3 ~  a1*ph_t2
> > > ph_t2 ~  a1* ph_t1
> > > '

messages.subject: using measEq.syntax() with the Industrialization and Political Democracy dataset
messages.subject_clean: using measEq.syntax() with the Industrialization and Political Democracy dataset
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I am using the Political Democracy dataset with the measEq.syntax() function as a pedagogical exercise. I take the model syntax for this dataset from Rosseel 2019.

I find that I cannot generate model syntax with measEq.syntax() that produces a reasonable fit. With the complete syntax:

mod.cat.complete <- '

# latent variable definitions
  ind60 =~ x1 + x2 + x3
  dem60 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4
  dem65 =~ y5 + y6 + y7 + y8

# regressions
  dem60 ~ ind60
  dem65 ~ ind60 + dem60

# residual (co)variances
  y1 ~~ y5
  y2 ~~ y4 + y6
  y3 ~~ y7
  y4 ~~ y8
  y6 ~~ y8
'
...the fit of course looks reasonable, but if I remove the residual (co)variances syntax I have this:

mod.cat.partial <- '

# latent variable definitions
  ind60 =~ x1 + x2 + x3
  dem60 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4
  dem65 =~ y5 + y6 + y7 + y8

# regressions
  dem60 ~ ind60
  dem65 ~ ind60 + dem60
'
...as the configural model in measEq.syntax():

syntax.partial <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = mod.cat.partial,
                               data = PoliticalDemocracy,
                               parameterization = "theta",
                               ID.fac = "marker",
                               ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016")

Then the fit statistics generated with:

syntax.partial.fit <- sem(as.character(syntax.partial),
                          data = PoliticalDemocracy)
summary(syntax.partial.fit)

...are considerably worse compared to what I see with:

mod.complete.fit <- sem(mod.cat.complete,
                           data = PoliticalDemocracy)
summary(mod.complete.fit)

I am wondering what I need to add to the syntax in mod.cat.partial in order to achieve a reasonable fit (short of providing the complete syntax)?

messages.body_plain:
Lucas

would suggest to add these arguments to see more information in the output

fit1 <- sem(mod_reg1, d, orthogonal = T, se="robust.huber.white", meanstructure=T)
summary(fit1, standardize=T, rsquare=T)

This way you willm see the intercepts as well, and see the standardize auto-regressive effects, and R2.

Yeah, it says that the aut-regressive effect is 0.6, how much T is predicted by T-1. And you do reject the null hypothesis of it being equal to 0. You cal also extend this interpretation by nclduing the standardize and R2 values

> > > > > #### phantom variables

> > > > > ph_t1 =~ NA*t1
> > > > > ph_t2 =~ NA*t2
> > > > > ph_t3 =~ NA*t3
> > > > > ## fix factor variances at 1

> > > > > ph_t2 ~~ 1*ph_t2
> > > > > ph_t3 ~~ 1*ph_t3
> > > > > ## fix factor means at 0

> > > > > ph_t2 ~0*1
> > > > > ph_t3 ~0*1
> > > > > ## fix indicator variances at 0. Meaning all the variance falls into the factor

> > > > > t2 ~~ 0*t2
> > > > > t3 ~~ 0*t3
> > > > > #### aut regression

There are myriad exclusion criteria one might justifiably rationalize, but I cannot possible automate (or even guess) them all.  However, I included a mechanism for users to be able to exclude whatever imputations (using whatever rule) with the omit.imps= argument to all lavaan.mi methods and dedicated functions.
See the description on the class?lavaan.mi help page:

Specific imputation numbers can also be included in this argument, in case users want to apply their own custom omission criteria (or simulations can use different numbers of imputations without redundantly refitting the model).

Automatically or manually selecting imputation numbers is up to the user, but automation could possibly be facilitated by the FUN= argument that runMI() passes to lavaanList()

messages.body_plain:
> what is the difference between “DWLS” and “WLSMV” estimators?

"WLSMV" is a keyword, not an estimator.  As the text states (which you pasted in your last post; see also the ?lavOptions help page), WLSMV implies DWLS.  Specifically, when you set (or rely on the default setting when declaring any outcomes as ordered=), estimator = "WLSMV" is a shortcut for the following three arguments:
estimator = "DWLS"
se = "robust.sem"
test = "scaled.shifted"
So if you explicitly only declare (1) without also declaring (2) and (3), that might be the source of your discrepancy.  You can always check your model results to verify:
lavInspect(fit, "options")[c("estimator","se","test")]

You need (2) and (3) to obtain robust results; otherwise, you cannot trust your test statistics or CIs to have nominal Type I error rates or CI coverage rates.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.body_plain:
First, this has nothing to do with measEq.syntax().  When you fix 6 parameters to zero (whose estimates are substantially nonzero) rather than estimating them, your model fit of course gets worse.  Just run the help-page example and then again omit the residual covariances to verify:

example(sem)
mod2 <- '# latent variable definitions

  ind60 =~ x1 + x2 + x3
  dem60 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4
  dem65 =~ y5 + y6 + y7 + y8

# regressions
  dem60 ~ ind60

  dem65 ~ ind60 + dem60 '
fit0 <- sem(mod2, data = PoliticalDemocracy)
summary(semTools::compareFit(fit, fit0))

Second, measEq.syntax() is for testing invariance in CFAs, so don't include regressions among common factors (the predictors might be misinterpreted as higher-order factors; read the help page).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

Hello,

I've recently estimated a structural equation model in lavaan using a weighted least squares estimator, since many of the indicators of the latent variables are categorical. I used the sampling.weights argument to incorporate a base weight to account for survey design before reading that lavaan (and lavaan.survey?) doesn't yet support the use of weights with a WLS estimator. When I ran the model, however, I didn't receive any error messages or indications that something was wrong and my output showed normal, error- and warning- free results. The weight variable is listed in the output, implying that it was used in the analysis without issue.

I understand that I probably shouldn't trust the results of the model since the lavaan manual says weights aren't supported with WLS but given the normal results, I'm not sure exactly why. I assume lavaan isn't properly incorporating the weights but how exactly is it estimating the model parameters when passed this unsupported model and in what ways are these results incorrect?

Thanks for your help

messages.body_plain:
> I am running a multilevel multigroup model comparing effects b/w younger and older siblings (“Birth Order”), accounting for nesting within families (“FamID”).

I don't think lavaan can do this.  Your grouping variable varies within clusters/families (Level 1).  The block structure in lavaan syntax in your MG-ML-SEM assumes the grouping variable is constant within clusters (Level 2).

It might be possible to implement MuML estimation in lavaan with a Level-1 grouping variable, but I have not implemented it, so please report back here if you are able to accomplish it.  Advantageously, it sounds like you have equal cluster sizes (2 siblings per family?), which MuML assumes.  This paper has the details:

https://doi.org/10.1080/00273171.2014.1003769

Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

Hello,

I am fitting a MGCFA with ULMSV and ordinal data. I am using an ESEM-CFA approach, i.e. using with factor loadings from previous EFA, items are allowed to cross-load factors in the model. I am interested in testing model invariance; my attempt:

# Model 1
es_configural <- as.character(measEq.syntax(esem_model, data = df, meanstructure = T,  estimator = "ULSMV", ordered = T, return.fit = T))

# Model 2
es_thresholds <- as.character(measEq.syntax(esem_model, data = df, meanstructure = T,  estimator = "ULSMV", ordered = T,   return.fit = T, group.equal = c("thresholds")))

# Model 3
es_metric <- as.character(measEq.syntax(esem_model, data = df, meanstructure = T,  estimator = "ULSMV", ordered = T,  return.fit = T,  group.equal = c("thresholds", "loadings")))

Results show that the three models are perfectly equivalent, same df, CFI, etc. Any idea why? I had warnings (The variance-covariance matrix of the estimated parameters (vcov) does not appear to be positive definite)

Thank you very much for your help

1 - lavInspect(fit, "est")$psi["dem65", "dem65"] / lavInspect(fit, "cov.lv <http://cov.lv>")["dem65", "dem65"]

in that case, because they depend on the original variance/covariance
matrix, which is going to compose different data in the two models.

With the same data, changing the model can move the AIC in either
direction, as it includes an adjustment for the number of parameters
estimated.

Pat

messages.subject_clean: AIC got worse with MLM estimator
messages.body_plain:
Generally, the difference test is preferred when the models being
compared are nested because its properties are well established. Note
that it does assume that the full (less-restricted) fits well,
generally interpreted as non-significant chi-squared. AIC and related
approaches (BIC, adjBIC) are more often used when the models being
compared are not nested, because the difference test does not apply to
that situation.

messages.body_plain:
Hello All,

I would like some help on how to get unstandardized values for my loadings in CFA as I want to calculate H and Omega? I don’t want the first loading to be 1 so I can calculate reliability for loadings and errors for my measure.

Thank you for your help.

Katalin

messages.subject: Re: Getting Unstandardized Values in CFA
messages.subject_clean: Getting Unstandardized Values in CFA
messages.body_plain:
Katalin

The estimates are always unstandardized, the difference is you method of factor identification. If you want to use fixed factor variance (having the factor variance equal to 1) instead of marker variable add the argument std.lv <http://std.lv>=T to the cfa call

Also, you can use the function reliability from the semTools package to estimate Omega

> > > > > > > > > You should use the function lavTestScore(weakmodel), these will do a LRT for each specific equality constraint in the model. So, you can identify if a single item may be problematic, if these is the case you can relase the equality constraint for only that 1 item. And if you are satisfied with that model, you can continue, this is called partial-measurement invariance. Its fine to continue if you have partial-invariance. The recommensation I make is to seek to have at least half the items being invariant to be able to make reliable inferences for latent parameters (like your growth curve). This comes from personla experience, I havent seen research suggesting a minimum threshold of items to be invariant

> > > > > > > > > > About combining the factor scores for the growth curve factors into your data set and use that in posterior analysis. This is NOT recommended. Regressions with factor scores will be bias, unless you do some method to account for correction, like Croon's bias correction, or plausible values. Just adding your estimated factor scores into your data set will give you bias regressions.

> > > > > > > > > > > > You should use the function lavTestScore(weakmodel), these will do a LRT for each specific equality constraint in the model. So, you can identify if a single item may be problematic, if these is the case you can relase the equality constraint for only that 1 item. And if you are satisfied with that model, you can continue, this is called partial-measurement invariance. Its fine to continue if you have partial-invariance. The recommensation I make is to seek to have at least half the items being invariant to be able to make reliable inferences for latent parameters (like your growth curve). This comes from personla experience, I havent seen research suggesting a minimum threshold of items to be invariant

messages.body_plain:
Dear Mauricio and other colleagues who might be following this thread,

You've been extremely helpful already and I really appreciate the time you've put in helping me. But, after some simulations and reading more about AR models in lavaan, I came to the conclusion that this is not quite what I'm looking for yet. I'll explain the issue in more detail below. If you're unable to help, though, I already truly appreciate the insights you've offered so far.

As I've mentioned before, I'm trying to replicate with SEM the results I obtain with the Anderson and Hsiao (1982) and Arellano (1989) estimators. In a nutshell, their model is a first differences model within an AR framework using the initial levels of the variable of interest as an instrument. I simulated some data and ran the approaches you suggested, as well as the Anderson-Hsiao/Arellano estimator below so that you hopefully will get a better idea of what I want.

To summarize my issue, the AR model in lavaan gives me an estimate of the autoregressor. This is fine, but I'm actually interested in the autoregressor of the differences between the values of the variable at different points in time. Put differently, I want to know if previous variation in variable X predict future  variations in X. Hopefully, the code will make that clearer than I've been able to put with words.

I know that these approaches are actually very similar. Indeed, as the simulation below indicates, both retrieve the true value of the coefficients quite well. The issue is that, on the real data, I'm obtaining different substantive results with lavaan from those with the Anderson-Hsiao/Arellano estimator. That's why I want to replicate the model as closely as possible, to ensure that my results are robust.

Here are my questions: is there a way to run a first differences model in lavaan? Is the package even built to deal with these kinds of model? I also checked the ctsem package you recommended. It seems to be the right one for my purposes, but I found their vignette <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ctsem/vignettes/hierarchicalmanual.pdf> extremely difficult to follow. After reading it, I have no idea how to define a model in the package.

Before moving on to the code, a couple of observations about it: what I'm really interested in doing is comparing the stability of two variables. I really want to be able to say: variable X is more stable over time than variable Z. That's what the code below simulates.

messages.subject: What does it mean when the Correlation between Slope and Intercept in a latent growth curve model is <1?
messages.subject_clean: What does it mean when the Correlation between Slope and Intercept in a latent growth curve model is <1?
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I try to do a multigroup analysis with a latent growth curve model in lavaan (see picture and syntax):

mod = '
Int =~  1*y1 + 1*y2 + 1*y3
Slo =~ 1*y1 + 2*y2 + 3*y3

Int ~~ Slo

Int  ~ X1 + country_2  # with country_1 as reference category)
Slo ~ X1 + country_2
X1 ~ country_2
X1 ~ 1
'
fit <- growth(mod, data = data, estimator='ML',
                        missing = "FIML", group = 'sex')

summary(fit, standardized = TRUE, fit.measures = TRUE)

The following Warning turns up at the end of the estimation:

"Warning message:In lav_start_check_cov(lavpartable = lavpartable, start = START) : lavaan WARNING: starting values imply a correlation larger than 1; variables involved are:  Int   Slo [in block 2]"

After first checkings, it turns out, that the problem of the correlation >1 between Intercept and Slope occurs only in a certain group (male) within country_2. If I omit either the regression of the intercept or the regression of the slope to the country variable, the multigroup model runs perfectly. Model fits are always very good (CFI>0.97) but the slopes are low and insignificant - so there seems to be no change over time. However, a LR test indicated that a random-intercept-random-slope model is significantly better than just a random-intercept-fixed slope model.

Now my Question is: What does it mean, when in a certain group the correlation between Intercept and Slope is estimated >1 as soon as a certain conditional variable is considered? Is this a problem of multicollinearity? It seems to me, that the whole issue is located in the following section of the model:

Let me know if you need further information. I would be very grateful for your help.

Best Wishes

Randy

messages.subject: WLSMV Interpreting probit coefficients and thresholds in terms of probability
messages.subject_clean: WLSMV Interpreting probit coefficients and thresholds in terms of probability
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am estimating a path model by using probit estimation (WLSMV).

In one equation, the dependent variable (Y1) is binary and the two (endogenous) predictors are continuous (X1 and X2). Knowing that it is a probit regression based on WLSMV and not a logit regression, my question is:

How could I interpret the results of this regression in terms of probability?

Here are the unstandardized parameters:
X1 : B1 = -.23
X2: B2 = .14
Threshold = .59

(I understand that the regression coefficients (B1 or B2) can be interpreted as the change in probit value of Y1* (latent response variable) for each 1 unit increase in X1 or X2 (respectively). I also understand that the threshold is the value of the latent response variable at which the observe binary variable switches from 0 to 1. )

Any help would be greatly appreciated!

Myriam

> > > > > > > > > > > > > You should use the function lavTestScore(weakmodel), these will do a LRT for each specific equality constraint in the model. So, you can identify if a single item may be problematic, if these is the case you can relase the equality constraint for only that 1 item. And if you are satisfied with that model, you can continue, this is called partial-measurement invariance. Its fine to continue if you have partial-invariance. The recommensation I make is to seek to have at least half the items being invariant to be able to make reliable inferences for latent parameters (like your growth curve). This comes from personla experience, I havent seen research suggesting a minimum threshold of items to be invariant

messages.body_plain:
Lucas

What you describe sounds like auto-regressions between latent change scores. But when I run that model with a simulated data it does not replicate the results from ivreg(). I think the issue is what the do with | z1
What would be the equivalent use of |z1 ?

Here is an example of the auto-regression model between change scores

library(AER)
library(lavaan)
library(tidyverse)

sim_data <- tibble(
     x1 = rnorm(1000),

     x2 = x1 + rnorm(1000),

     x3 = x2 + rnorm(1000),

     z1 = rnorm(1000),

     z2 = 1.5 * z1 + rnorm(1000),

     z3 = 1.5 * z2 + rnorm(1000)

   )

### latent change score
### T2 - T1
### T3 - T2
change321_mod <- '
### latent true scores
PT1 =~ 1*z1
PT2 =~ 1*z2
PT3 =~ 1*z3

PT1 ~~ NA*PT1
PT2 ~~ 0*PT2
PT3 ~~ 0*PT3

PT1 ~1
PT2 ~0*1
PT3 ~0*1

z1 ~0*1
z2 ~0*1
z3 ~0*1

z1 ~~ uv*z1
z2 ~~ uv*z2
z3 ~~ uv*z3

### autoregressions
PT2 ~ 1*PT1
PT3 ~ 1*PT2

### latent change scores
change_21 =~ 1*PT2
change_32 =~ 1*PT3

change_21 ~c(m21)*1
change_32 ~c(m32)*1

### dynamic noise
change_21 ~~ c(v21)*change_21
change_32 ~~ c(v32)*change_32

### autoregressions of change scores
change_32 ~ change_21
change_21 ~ PT1
'

fit321 <- cfa(change321_mod, data=sim_data, orthogonal=T)
summary(fit321, standardized=T,rsquare=T)

On Thursday, January 14, 2021 at 8:54:19 PM UTC+1 ldea...@ucsd.edu wrote:
> Dear Mauricio and other colleagues who might be following this thread,
>
> You've been extremely helpful already and I really appreciate the time you've put in helping me. But, after some simulations and reading more about AR models in lavaan, I came to the conclusion that this is not quite what I'm looking for yet. I'll explain the issue in more detail below. If you're unable to help, though, I already truly appreciate the insights you've offered so far.
>
> As I've mentioned before, I'm trying to replicate with SEM the results I obtain with the Anderson and Hsiao (1982) and Arellano (1989) estimators. In a nutshell, their model is a first differences model within an AR framework using the initial levels of the variable of interest as an instrument. I simulated some data and ran the approaches you suggested, as well as the Anderson-Hsiao/Arellano estimator below so that you hopefully will get a better idea of what I want.
>
> To summarize my issue, the AR model in lavaan gives me an estimate of the autoregressor. This is fine, but I'm actually interested in the autoregressor of the differences between the values of the variable at different points in time. Put differently, I want to know if previous variation in variable X predict future  variations in X. Hopefully, the code will make that clearer than I've been able to put with words.
>
> I know that these approaches are actually very similar. Indeed, as the simulation below indicates, both retrieve the true value of the coefficients quite well. The issue is that, on the real data, I'm obtaining different substantive results with lavaan from those with the Anderson-Hsiao/Arellano estimator. That's why I want to replicate the model as closely as possible, to ensure that my results are robust.
>
> Here are my questions: is there a way to run a first differences model in lavaan? Is the package even built to deal with these kinds of model? I also checked the ctsem package you recommended. It seems to be the right one for my purposes, but I found their vignette <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ctsem/vignettes/hierarchicalmanual.pdf> extremely difficult to follow. After reading it, I have no idea how to define a model in the package.
>

> > > > > > > t2 ~ a1*t1
> > > > > > > '
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > 2. You standardized the variables at each time point by creating phantom factors, and express the variance differences in the factor loadings, and mean differences in the indicator means
> > > > > > > mod_reg2 <- '
> > > > > > > #### phantom variables
> > > > > > > ## estimate factor loadings: standard deviations at each time point
> > > > > > > ph_t1 =~ NA*t1
> > > > > > > ph_t2 =~ NA*t2
> > > > > > > ph_t3 =~ NA*t3
> > > > > > > ## fix factor variances at 1
> > > > > > > ph_t1 ~~ 1*ph_t1
> > > > > > > ph_t2 ~~ 1*ph_t2
> > > > > > > ph_t3 ~~ 1*ph_t3
> > > > > > > ## fix factor means at 0
> > > > > > > ph_t1 ~0*1
> > > > > > > ph_t2 ~0*1
> > > > > > > ph_t3 ~0*1
> > > > > > > ## fix indicator variances at 0. Meaning all the variance falls into the factor
> > > > > > > t1 ~~ 0*t1
> > > > > > > t2 ~~ 0*t2
> > > > > > > t3 ~~ 0*t3
> > > > > > > #### aut regression
> > > > > > > ph_t3 ~  a1*ph_t2
> > > > > > > ph_t2 ~  a1* ph_t1
> > > > > > > '

> > > > > > > > > > > > I'm trying to use a measurement model to estimate the stability of a variable across multiple measurements. . Largely, I'm trying to approximate the results obtained using a dynamic model approach. For those not familiar with it, dynamic panels are, basically, a first differences model, using the lagged levels of the variable as an instrument In a nutshell, the closer  to 0 the value of the slope, the more stable the variable is.
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > I seek to do a similar thing using Lavaan but I'm unsure about how to go about it–unsure about how to interpret the results or even if what I'm doing is right, even after reading the Lavaan tutorial <https://urldefense.com/v3/__https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/tutorial.pdf__;!!Mih3wA!TPuVEbcYLFwmgnoFO7N9437nCXuh1kbtfKvT26eaPNZC0T87WAuG0F6Qdu9Gz8DS$>.
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > Suppose I have a three wave panel, where variable x is measured at t1, t2, and t3. I simply want to get at the stability of x, for now–i.e., the simplest possible model. Here's what I have, so far:
> > > > > > > > > > > >

> > > > > > > > > > > > "

> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > I get results, but I'm unsure about how to interpret them. What is the hypotheses being tested in the parameters?
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > Per reading the tutorial, I tried using labels to make t2 equal to t3, but I'm not at all sure this is what I want. I'm also unsure whether I should use growth(), rather than sem(), though they do not seem to be very different from each other.
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > Any help would be much appreciated.
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > Thank you and happy holydays to all,

Manuel

##

When looking at the estimates they sometimes have different operators (+/-) than in the manifest correlation matrix (see attached pdf). Also different constructs get significant. Is this because of the latent construct modeling or am I doing something wrong / misinterpreting the estimates?

##
I dont see any syntax issues here. So, I would tend to think that the differences are due to looking at relations between observed and latent variables. Also, after you have strong invariance

##

In a second step I added the correlations to the boredom growth model:

Looking at the output (see attached pdf) the intercept now only correlates significantly with KC27sc_T.

##
Now, these relations have no similar with manifest variables, as you dont have a measure intercept/slope. But relating them to characteristics of change. So, wouldnt be sorprise if the relations are "different"

Glad this has help

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > You should use the function lavTestScore(weakmodel), these will do a LRT for each specific equality constraint in the model. So, you can identify if a single item may be problematic, if these is the case you can relase the equality constraint for only that 1 item. And if you are satisfied with that model, you can continue, this is called partial-measurement invariance. Its fine to continue if you have partial-invariance. The recommensation I make is to seek to have at least half the items being invariant to be able to make reliable inferences for latent parameters (like your growth curve). This comes from personla experience, I havent seen research suggesting a minimum threshold of items to be invariant

messages.subject: Re: What does it mean when the Correlation between Slope and Intercept in a latent growth curve model is <1?
messages.subject_clean: What does it mean when the Correlation between Slope and Intercept in a latent growth curve model is <1?
messages.body_plain:
Randy

A couple things

mod = '
Int =~  1*y1 + 1*y2 + 1*y3

Slo =~ 0*y1 + 1*y2 + 2*y3
## usually you would put 0 as the first loading for the slope.
## you can put the 0 anywhere you want, but where in time the 0 is located is the time that the intercept is located for interpretation

Int ~~ Slo

Int  ~ X1 + country_2  # with country_1 as reference category)
Slo ~ X1 + country_2
X1 ~ country_2

X1 ~ 1 ## this line is unneccesary
'
Since I cant see your data, make sure the categorical variable is binary 0/1, so it can be use this way

If the high correlation shows conditional of a group variable would be that that is the most likely correlation for the reference group

With a high correlation between intercept and slope, would indicate that: the higher the starting point the higher the rate of change

##

Model fits are always very good (CFI>0.97) but the slopes are low and insignificant - so there seems to be no change over time. However, a LR test indicated that a random-intercept-random-slope model is significantly better than just a random-intercept-fixed slope model.

##
when you tested for  random-intercept-fixed slope model, you are still estimating a slope, so they are not very different ones. If you wanted to test Mean slope equal to 0, would have to add Slo ~0*1

messages.body_plain:
Greeting
Simply instal semTools package then After fitting your model in lavaan use the reliability function from semTools to compute AVE and CR.

for example:

library(lavaan)
library(semTools)

CFA.2F <-'F1=~ PVD2+PVD5+PVD6+PVD8+PVD10+PVD12+PVD14
          F2=~ PVD1+PVD3+PVD4+PVD7+PVD9+PVD11+PVD13+PVD15'

CFA.2F.sus <- cfa(CFA.2F, data = sus1,std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE,ordered=names(sus1), estimator = "WLSMV")

summary(CFA.2F.sus , fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)
# what you need
print(reliability(CFA.2F.sus,return.total = TRUE), digits = 3)

messages.subject: Re: What does it mean when the Correlation between Slope and Intercept in a latent growth curve model is <1?
messages.subject_clean: What does it mean when the Correlation between Slope and Intercept in a latent growth curve model is <1?
messages.body_plain:
Randy

When looking at a correlation out of bounds (std.all), like it seems this might be the case, you would first need to see if its an estimation problem or sample limitation.
So, a sample limitation would be that in you rcase you are working with multiple groups and binary covariates, so the correlation represents the partial correlation in function of this binary variable. Check the crosstable of sample size for multiple group*binary variable, if the sample size for some of the groups is very small might be that you are asking too big of a model for small samples.
On the other side, if you dont see any other estimation problem (eignevalues, very large SE, etc), would be good to check if the correlation is significantly different from 1. Meaning that you want to see if the inference would say that the correlation is very far from the extreme (if the correlation is 1.89 seems very far from 1). You could argue that the estimation is still fine but the out of bounds values are needed to estimate the best solution

Kolenikov, S., & Bollen, K. A. (2012). Testing Negative Error Variances: Is a Heywood Case a Symptom of Misspecification? Sociological Methods & Research, 41(1), 124–167. https://doi.org/10.1177/0049124112442138
Savalei, V., & Kolenikov, S. (2008). Constrained versus unconstrained estimation in structural equation modeling. Psychological Methods, 13(2), 150–170. https://doi.org/10.1037/1082-989X.13.2.150

Now, the interpretation of a high correlation between growth factors is different than from a CFA. In a CFA you would talk about the factor beng similar between them and might indicate that needs to use 1 factor instead of 2. But in a growth curve you cant say that because the factor are now describing the grwoth over time. So, you could say that the participants with higher intercept also presented the largerst increase over time, the factors are still different, but describing the conditional relation between them over time

 Could you include paste here the output to see it in more detail?

hope this makes sense

messages.subject: Re: WLSMV Interpreting probit coefficients and thresholds in terms of probability
messages.subject_clean: WLSMV Interpreting probit coefficients and thresholds in terms of probability
messages.body_plain:
> How could I interpret the results of this regression in terms of probability?

You mean like logistic regression slopes can be converted to odds ratios?  You can't.  The effect on probability is nonlinear.

> I understand that the regression coefficients (B1 or B2) can be interpreted as the change in probit value of Y1* (latent response variable) for each 1 unit increase in X1 or X2 (respectively).

There is no single number that describes the change in P(Y=1 | X) per unit change in X.  There is a linear / additive change in Y1* (probit), or in logistic regression, a linear / additive change in the logit OR a multiplicative change in odds.

If X were a grouping variable, you could calculate the expected probability in each group and calculate your own risk ratio.  Likewise, for continuous X you could choose any 2 representative values of X and calculate the expected probabilities, to calculate a risk ratio for those 2 levels of X.

> I also understand that the threshold is the value of the latent response variable at which the observe binary variable switches from 0 to 1. )

Right.  So if you used the default delta parameterization, then 0.59 is a z score (because Y1* has unit variance) beyond which Y=1.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

Thank you all for your positive feedback. @Terrence, I am thinking about implementing 3 features:

(1) Calculate confidence intervals from a fitted bootstrapLavaan object. Something like this:

HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9'

fit <- sem(HS.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939)
res <- bootstrapLavaan(fit, FUN = "coef", ...)
newBootFunction(object = res, conf = 0.95, type = "bca")

                ci.lower ci.upper
visual=~x2        0.3300   0.8825
visual=~x3        0.4946   1.1032
textual=~x5       0.9957   1.2626
...

This should also work with a custom FUN.

(2) There is obviously not very much information in the fitted bootstrapLavaan object. From there I would like to work supplementary with a wrapper to be able to provide some extra information. Like this:

newBootFunction(object = fit, ... (args for bootstrapLavaan), conf = 0.95, type = "bca")

                   coef    bias     se ci.lower ci.upper
visual=~x1       1.0000      NA     NA   1.0000   1.0000
visual=~x2       0.5535  0.0141 0.1426   0.3300   0.8825
visual=~x3       0.7294  0.0112 0.1534   0.4946   1.1032
...

A custom FUN should be usable here as well.

(3) Assuming different coefficients should be bootstrapped with a single bootstrap run (parameterEstimates, standardizedSolution, semTools::HTMT, ...), this would of course be possible with a custom FUN, but probably quite hard to implement for a less experienced user. That's why I would like to add something like this:

newBootFunction(object = fit, ... (args for bootstrapLavaan), out = c("parameterEstimates", "standardizedSolution", ...), conf = 0.95, type = "bca")

$parameterEstimates
                   coef    bias     se ci.lower ci.upper
visual=~x1       1.0000      NA     NA   1.0000   1.0000
visual=~x2       0.5535  0.0141 0.1426   0.3300   0.8825
visual=~x3       0.7294  0.0112 0.1534   0.4946   1.1032
...

$standardizedSolution
...

$`semTools::HTMT`
...

At least these are my current ideas. Perhaps a matrix representation of the results would also be useful, if one or more matrices are bootstrapped. It may well be that I am thinking in the wrong direction. Comments and criticism are very welcome.

or do I need to interact with each constructs like this: INT ~ inc*A + inc*SN + inc*PBC

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have a naïve question.   I want to model my experimental conditions (X, Y) as 2 different factors in a mediation analysis with latent variables. Is there any problem if either the outcome (Y) or the mediator variable have only one latent variable? There are 2 scenarios on this regard:
model1 <- '
   # latent variables
   X =~ x1 + x2
   M =~ m1 + m2 + m3
   Y =~ y1
           # direct effect
             Y ~ c*X
           # mediator
             M ~ a*X
             Y ~ b*M
           # indirect effect (a*b)
             ab := a*b
           # total effect
             total := c + (a*b)
         '
model2 <- '
   # latent variables
   X =~ x1 + x2
   M =~ m1
   Y =~ y1 + y2
           # direct effect
             Y ~ c*X
           # mediator
             M ~ a*X
             Y ~ b*M
           # indirect effect (a*b)
             ab := a*b
           # total effect
             total := c + (a*b)
         '
Thanks in advance for your comments.

Best,

On Saturday, December 2, 2017 at 3:41:27 PM UTC-8 Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> > Is it possible to obtain the p-Value / Wald-z Statistik from the R output
>
> Yes, if you define a new parameter as the difference between those parameters.  This is similar to defining indirect effects as products of individual paths:
>
> http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/mediation.html
>
> You could also constrain the paths to equality across groups by giving them the same label, then comparing that restricted model to the model without the restriction, using the lavTestLRT() function.

> http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/groups.html
>

Latent change score models create phantom factors ( change_21 and change_32 in this case). These factor represent the difference between 2 time points, and the I added auto-regressions between them.

> > > > > > > > > Ok, an autoregressor model with SEM could be done in a couple of different ways.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > 1. You maintain the metric and scale for the the original variable scales. This one could be done directly using the variables. With a lag 1 regression between them, we are labeling this AR1 regression a1 so that we are stating that stability effect is the same between time points
> > > > > > > > > mod_reg1 <- '
> > > > > > > > > t3 ~ a1*t2
> > > > > > > > > t2 ~ a1*t1
> > > > > > > > > '
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > 2. You standardized the variables at each time point by creating phantom factors, and express the variance differences in the factor loadings, and mean differences in the indicator means
> > > > > > > > > mod_reg2 <- '
> > > > > > > > > #### phantom variables
> > > > > > > > > ## estimate factor loadings: standard deviations at each time point
> > > > > > > > > ph_t1 =~ NA*t1
> > > > > > > > > ph_t2 =~ NA*t2
> > > > > > > > > ph_t3 =~ NA*t3
> > > > > > > > > ## fix factor variances at 1
> > > > > > > > > ph_t1 ~~ 1*ph_t1
> > > > > > > > > ph_t2 ~~ 1*ph_t2
> > > > > > > > > ph_t3 ~~ 1*ph_t3
> > > > > > > > > ## fix factor means at 0
> > > > > > > > > ph_t1 ~0*1
> > > > > > > > > ph_t2 ~0*1
> > > > > > > > > ph_t3 ~0*1
> > > > > > > > > ## fix indicator variances at 0. Meaning all the variance falls into the factor
> > > > > > > > > t1 ~~ 0*t1
> > > > > > > > > t2 ~~ 0*t2
> > > > > > > > > t3 ~~ 0*t3
> > > > > > > > > #### aut regression
> > > > > > > > > ph_t3 ~  a1*ph_t2
> > > > > > > > > ph_t2 ~  a1* ph_t1
> > > > > > > > > '
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > 3. The third options I would recommend is to use ctsem for continuous time panel models (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ctsem/index.html <https://urldefense.com/v3/__https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ctsem/index.html__;!!Mih3wA!XXrXPpm22V_0aDy8V3qTtHMfImn_ki7y-nOvsCtC-mKr6vyThAHDV2j3M8mSygdn$>)

messages.body_plain:
When you add the time invariant covariate like this, you are constraining it to have the same effect (Age label) across time and variables. I would recommend to have it constraint across time, but not across variables
##

# Regression of random intercepts on Age as time-invariant predictor
  ix1 + ix2 + iy1 +iy2 + iy3 ~ Age*s1 # Constrained over time.
##

Like this
ix1 ~ Agex*s1
ix2 ~ Agex*s1
iy1 ~ Agey*s1
iy2 ~ Agey*s1

You can always allow it to be different over time, and compare the models

I havent use the RI models before, so I will assume that part is correct

As the within time covariances are constraint to be equal, this is assuming the residual correlation is equal. This seems like an overly restrictive constraint to me, to could allow these covariances to be different over time.

About the moderation, you could build the latent factor interaction at each time point. With either double mean centering or residual cenering. You can do this with the ?indProd function from semTools.
Basically,
- the initial model need to have also the covariate predicting Ra
- create an interaction of indicators for Fe and the covariate.
- Then you cadd another latent variable that is define by these interaction indicators
- add the covariate and the latent interaction as predictors of Ra over time
- then evaluate the signifficance of the latent interaction factor
- evaluate the magnitude of its effect by the change in R2 when the factor indicator is added
- test for simple slopes with the probe2Way functions from semTools (make sure to use the one respective to same type of indicator interaction you used)
- plot the desire simple slopes with the plotProbe function from semTools

Hope this helps

messages.subject_clean: Adding interaction terms
messages.body_plain:
Nam

Sadly the answer is "it depends".

If you want to talk in the "common" use of a covariate variable, if you want to make it equivalent to linear regression you add it as a predictor only for the main regression. If you want to control for its effect on all the model, you add it as a predictor for all the factors.
You would add the interactions only if you are interested in the change of slope as a function of the coavriates

As a side not, you cannot add interactions like that in lavaan, there you are labeling the regressions, not adding an interaction. Given that you have latent variables you would have to create a latent interaction factor with double mean center or residual center interaction indicators. Check the indprod() function from semTools for this

> > > > > > > > > > mod_reg1 <- '

> > > > > > > > > > t2 ~ a1*t1
> > > > > > > > > > '
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > 2. You standardized the variables at each time point by creating phantom factors, and express the variance differences in the factor loadings, and mean differences in the indicator means
> > > > > > > > > > mod_reg2 <- '
> > > > > > > > > > #### phantom variables
> > > > > > > > > > ## estimate factor loadings: standard deviations at each time point
> > > > > > > > > > ph_t1 =~ NA*t1
> > > > > > > > > > ph_t2 =~ NA*t2
> > > > > > > > > > ph_t3 =~ NA*t3
> > > > > > > > > > ## fix factor variances at 1
> > > > > > > > > > ph_t1 ~~ 1*ph_t1
> > > > > > > > > > ph_t2 ~~ 1*ph_t2
> > > > > > > > > > ph_t3 ~~ 1*ph_t3
> > > > > > > > > > ## fix factor means at 0
> > > > > > > > > > ph_t1 ~0*1
> > > > > > > > > > ph_t2 ~0*1
> > > > > > > > > > ph_t3 ~0*1
> > > > > > > > > > ## fix indicator variances at 0. Meaning all the variance falls into the factor
> > > > > > > > > > t1 ~~ 0*t1
> > > > > > > > > > t2 ~~ 0*t2
> > > > > > > > > > t3 ~~ 0*t3
> > > > > > > > > > #### aut regression
> > > > > > > > > > ph_t3 ~  a1*ph_t2
> > > > > > > > > > ph_t2 ~  a1* ph_t1
> > > > > > > > > > '

On Tuesday, January 19, 2021 at 11:12:11 AM UTC+1 mauga...@gmail.com wrote:
> Nam
>
> Sadly the answer is "it depends".
>
> If you want to talk in the "common" use of a covariate variable, if you want to make it equivalent to linear regression you add it as a predictor only for the main regression. If you want to control for its effect on all the model, you add it as a predictor for all the factors.
> You would add the interactions only if you are interested in the change of slope as a function of the coavriates
>
> As a side not, you cannot add interactions like that in lavaan, there you are labeling the regressions, not adding an interaction. Given that you have latent variables you would have to create a latent interaction factor with double mean center or residual center interaction indicators. Check the indprod() function from semTools for this
>
>
>
> On Monday, January 18, 2021 at 7:55:39 PM UTC+1 dangvu...@gmail.com wrote:

> > SEMtpbmodel <- '
> >
> >    # latent variables
> >
> > A =~ att1 + att2
> >

> >

> >    # regressions

> > Should I add, for instance inc (income), to each construct (A, SN, PBC)? Or add to the main regression only: INT ~ A + SN + PBC + inc ?

> > or do I need to interact with each constructs like this: INT ~ inc*A + inc*SN + inc*PBC
> >
> > I look forward to your advice.
> >
> > Thank you in advance!
> >
> > Nam

messages.body_plain:
Hi Terrence,

I really appreciate the clarifications. If you don't mind 2 follow-up questions:

1. About thresholds

> Right.  So if you used the default delta parameterization, then 0.59 is a z score (because Y1* has unit variance) beyond which Y=1.

In this model I used theta parameterization, so it's the residual variance of Y1* that has unit variance, right? In that case, I imagine that the threshold cannot be interpreted as a z score, but is there another meaningful way that I can interpret the threshold besides what was described above? (i.e., the threshold is the value of the latent response variable at which the observed binary variable switches from 0 to 1).

2. Scales y*
Am I right to think that in my output, the coefficient under "Scales y*" is the estimated variance of the y* variable? (Since in theta parameterization, it's the residual variance that is fixed at 1.)

Also, just wanted to thank you for, and highlight for others in my situation, the PPT handout posted in another conversation on measurement equivalence in models with categorical indicators <https://www.uva.nl/binaries/content/documents/personalpages/j/o/t.d.jorgensen/en/tab-three/tab-three/cpitem%5B2%5D/asset?1556027804259>. Super useful to clarify identification trade-offs for thresholds/variance /intercepts and some differences between delta and theta parameterization.

Best,
Myriam

From past posts, I think there would be some interest in preprogrammed routines for bootstrapping a set of particular results.  Depending on the choice of out= argument, the ... arguments could also be passed to bootstrapLRT(), which additionally involves the model-based ("Bollen-Stine") transformation. > Perhaps a matrix representation of the results would also be useful, if one or more matrices are bootstrapped

Perhaps, then, the out= function could take arguments to lavInspect().  Rather than "parameterEstimates" (which is a function that returns many values beyond what is needed), it could be either "coef" (a vector, like your current output example) or "est" (the estimates in LISREL matrices, and the output could be character strings of "lower ; upper" bounds). messages.body_plain:
> In this model I used theta parameterization, so it's the residual variance of Y1* that has unit variance, right? In that case, I imagine that the threshold cannot be interpreted as a z score, but is there another meaningful way that I can interpret the threshold besides what was described above?

Yes, Y1* is simply not a z score (its SD > 1).

> (i.e., the threshold is the value of the latent response variable at which the observed binary variable switches from 0 to 1).

Right, you answered your own question.  You can print the fully standardized solution (std.all) if you want to know the standardized threshold (the z score above which Y1* is classified in the higher category).  Or equivalently, Y1 = 1 when Y1* exceeds the unstandardized threshold, and the SD of Y1* is the reciprocal of its scale parameter.

> 2. Scales y*
> Am I right to think that in my output, the coefficient under "Scales y*" is the estimated variance of the y* variable? (Since in theta parameterization, it's the residual variance that is fixed at 1.)

No, it is the reciprocal of the marginal SD.  So if the y* scale parameter is 0.5, the marginal/total SD of y* is 1/0.5 = 2.

messages.subject: SEM, Binary DV, low CFI
messages.subject_clean: SEM, Binary DV, low CFI
messages.body_plain:
I have a model with three latent variables (four, five, and eight indicators) as predictors and one binary outcome. I am using a DWLS estimator. Binary DV is a decision to donate or not in different ocasions. I have three different studies but the model is same across studies.

In one study, I have 450 participants who donated and 70 who did not. I read that a high difference in number of participants between categories in binary DV should not be a problem for SEM. However, I am wondering can this big difference cause low robust CFI?

Is it recommendable at all to use SEM if the number of participants in one of categories in binary DV is small (in my case only 70)? Should I maybe opt for path analysis or logistic regression?

In another two samples, the overall number of participants is low: 136:30 and 91:28 (donated:did not donate). I guess in this case it would be best to switch to path analysis or logistic regression?

Thank you!

Aneta

Thanks!

Aneta

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I am working on a pathway analysis of 3 continuous latent variables and one categorical outcome variable.
The following is my code:

model <- '
# latent variable definitions
  # exogenous variable
l1 =~ 1*CTQ_SA + CTQ_PA + CTQ_EA + CTQ_EN + CTQ_PN
  # endogenous variables
l2 =~ 1*ECR_av10 + ECR_anx10
l3 =~ 1*YSQ_DR + YSQ_IA + YSQ_OD

# regressions
l2 ~ l1
l3 ~ l2
RV ~ l3

# covariances
l1~~l1
l2~~l2
l3~~l3
RV~~RV '

fit<- sem(model, data=data, meanstructure = TRUE, ordered = c("RV"))

and I get the following warning messages:
1: In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
  lavaan WARNING:
    Could not compute standard errors! The information matrix could
    not be inverted. This may be a symptom that the model is not
    identified.
2: In lav_test_satorra_bentler(lavobject = NULL, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
  lavaan WARNING: could not invert information matrix needed for robust test statistic

This is the first time I am using R and also the first time I am doing a pathway analysis, so I'd appreciate any help or tips to resolve these issues!

  '

A=~a1
B=~b1+b2
C=~c1+c2+c3+c4
D=~d1+d2
    '
fit <- cfa(model = measurement_model, data = data)

STEP2:
full_sem_model<-
  '
#measurement model
A=~a1
B=~b1+b2
C=~c1+c2+c3+c4
D=~d1+d2
    '
#regressions
A~B+Age
B~Gender + Age + A
C~A+Age
............(this is just example)
```

Trimmed model

messages.subject: Using polychoric covariance matrix as input instead of WLSMV or MLR
messages.subject_clean: Using polychoric covariance matrix as input instead of WLSMV or MLR
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am working with ordered data with 4 response categories. I have p(p+1)/2 = 45 information and 39 parameters to be estimated using WLSMV, 27 parameters to be estimated using MLR.

When I use WLSMV, I get a warning that the smallest eigenvalue is close to zero and that the model may not be identified (but all parameters including standard errors are estimated and in a sensible range). Using MLR, there are no warnings or errors. The parameter estimates are quite similar between both models, fit indices are fine (WLSMV has a slightly better fit), so I would come to the same conclusion independent of the model I choose.

I had the (maybe stupid?) idea of using using lavCov() to create a polychoric covariance matrix that I then can use as an input for ML estimation so I can at least partly account for the ordinal nature of the data. It works without problems, I obtain even better fit indices, similar parameter estimates, so again, I would come to the same conclusion.

So I was wondering what you would suggest as the best method? Can I ignore the warning, as estimation seems to be okay? Or is it sensible to use the polychoric covariance matrix, as this way the covariances that are used for estimation reflect the data better? Or would you go for an MLR estimation that allows for robust standard errors? I would be very happy for your ideas and suggestions!

Best Mirka

messages.subject: Re: Including missing with DWLS
messages.subject_clean: Including missing with DWLS
messages.body_plain:
For the first question, yes, missing="pairwise" is usually the best option for DWLS. It's using all measures. It analyzes the polychoric correlation matrix, where each correlation coefficient in the matrix is based on all respondents who provided data to both variables going into that coefficient. This set of respondents may vary coefficient to coefficient, which can lead to estimation problems if you have a lot of missing.

Reasons to choose DWLS vs MML I'll leave to those better qualified.

Pat
