messages.subject_clean: Help for a complex multilevel moderated mediation
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am working on a multilevel moderated mediation and I decided to use the lavaan package. I briefly describe the data I have (I added also the dataframe):

- time: one categorical predictor (two levels)
- memory task: continuous dependent variable,
- anxiety and depression: continuous mediators
- age: continuous moderator
- group: categorical moderator (three levels)

I attach the general model I would like to test (upper path diagram), also with the path coefficients (lower path diagram):

It is possible to generate them by using the folowing code:
library(processR)
labels=list(X="Time",M=c("Anx","Dep"),Y="Y")
moderator=list(name=c("Age","Group_cat1","Group_cat2"),
               matrix=list(c(1,1,0,1,1,1),c(0,0,0,0,1,1),c(0,0,0,0,1,1)),
               pos=c(1,2,4))

drawConcept(labels=labels,parallel=TRUE,moderator=moderator)
drawModel(labels=labels,parallel=TRUE,moderator=moderator,drawbox = F)

As far I can understand, a way to deal with categorical data is to convert them into dummy coded (0/1) variables. If the variable has k levels, it is possible to create k-1 dummy coded variables OR it could be performed a multigroup analysis. I tried to apply the first way for the "Group" moderator (taking Group B as reference for both comparisons). I attach the formula I would like to pass to lavaan:

eq='
Anx~a1*Time+a2*Age+a3*Time:Age
Dep~a4*Time+a5*Age+a6*Time:Age
Y~b1*Anx+b2*Age+b3*Anx:Age+b4*Group_cat1+b5*Anx:Group_cat1+b6*Group_cat2+b7*Anx:Group_cat2+b8*Dep+b9*Dep:Age+b10*Dep:Group_cat1+b11*Dep:Group_cat2+c1*Time+c2*Age+c3*Time:Age
Age ~ Age.mean*1
Age ~~ Age.var*Age

Group_cat1 ~ Group_cat1.mean*1
Group_cat1 ~~ Group_cat1.var*Group_cat1

Group_cat2 ~ Group_cat2.mean*1
Group_cat2 ~~ Group_cat2.var*Group_cat2

# Indirect Effect(s)

indirect1 := (a1+a3*Age.mean)*(b1+b3*Age.mean+b5*Group_cat1.mean+b7*Group_cat2.mean)
direct1 :=c1+c3*Age.mean
indirect1.below :=(a1+a3*(Age.mean-sqrt(Age.var)))*(b1+b3*(Age.mean-sqrt(Age.var))+b5*(Group_cat1.mean-sqrt(Group_cat1.var))+b7*(Group_cat2.mean-sqrt(Group_cat2.var)))
indirect1.above :=(a1+a3*(Age.mean+sqrt(Age.var)))*(b1+b3*(Age.mean+sqrt(Age.var))+b5*(Group_cat1.mean+sqrt(Group_cat1.var))+b7*(Group_cat2.mean+sqrt(Group_cat2.var)))
direct1.below:=c1+c3*(Age.mean-sqrt(Age.var))
direct1.above:=c1+c3*(Age.mean+sqrt(Age.var))
total1.below := direct1.below + indirect1.below
total1.above := direct1.above + indirect1.above
prop.mediated1.below := indirect1.below / total1.below
prop.mediated1.above := indirect1.above / total1.above

indirect2 := (a4+a6*Age.mean)*(b8+b9*Age.mean+b10*Group_cat1.mean+b11*Group_cat2.mean)
direct2 :=c1+c3*Age.mean
indirect2.below :=(a4+a6*(Age.mean-sqrt(Age.var)))*(b8+b9*(Age.mean-sqrt(Age.var))+b10*(Group_cat1.mean-sqrt(Group_cat1.var))+b11*(Group_cat2.mean-sqrt(Group_cat2.var)))
indirect2.above :=(a4+a6*(Age.mean+sqrt(Age.var)))*(b8+b9*(Age.mean+sqrt(Age.var))+b10*(Group_cat1.mean+sqrt(Group_cat1.var))+b11*(Group_cat2.mean+sqrt(Group_cat2.var)))
direct2.below:=c1+c3*(Age.mean-sqrt(Age.var))
direct2.above:=c1+c3*(Age.mean+sqrt(Age.var))
total2.below := direct2.below + indirect2.below
total2.above := direct2.above + indirect2.above
prop.mediated2.below := indirect2.below / total2.below
prop.mediated2.above := indirect2.above / total2.above

# Specific Indirect Effect Contrast(s)

Contrast1 := indirect1-indirect2

# Indirect/Direct/Total Effect(s)

indirect := indirect1+indirect2
direct := c1+c3*Age.mean
total := indirect + direct
prop.mediated := indirect / total
'

mymodel=sem(model=eq,data = df)
summary( mymodel )

In other words, I would like understand if the average time differences in Y are mediated by anx and dep scores and if this effect is moderated by the age of the respondents. Furthermore, I would like to understand if there is a moderation of the groups on the path between the mediators and Y.

First issue: Am I treating correctly the categotical variables?

Second issue: I would like to convert this model SEM (if correctly written) into a multilevel one, since this is a repeated measure design. I am completely stuck on how to code the within/random part of the model. If I used a linear mixed effect model, I would set the ID as clustering variable and random intercepts and slopes (time|ID maybe).

I am sorry for the long post. Could you give me some help on how to rewrite my eq formula in multilevel term? Every suggestion would be precious.

Thank you in advance for your time and availability

Best Regards,

Umberto

messages.subject: Re: Using polychoric covariance matrix as input instead of WLSMV or MLR
messages.subject_clean: Using polychoric covariance matrix as input instead of WLSMV or MLR
messages.body_plain:
> I had the (maybe stupid?) idea of using using lavCov() to create a polychoric covariance matrix that I then can use as an input for ML estimation

You can't trust the SEs or test statistics because they treat the polychorics as known observations rather than as estimates (with their own SEs).  Taking the uncertainty of the first-step estimates into account is what DWLS does.

> I was wondering what you would suggest as the best method?

Depends how you define "best", and what your sample size is, and some other properties of the observed data, and some properties of the assumed latent responses if you use DWLS.

> Can I ignore the warning, as estimation seems to be okay?

 Probably, if there are no other signs of empirical underidentification.

> Or is it sensible to use the polychoric covariance matrix, as this way the covariances that are used for estimation reflect the data better?

You cannot compare fit across those estimators because they are based on different (assumptions about the) data.  Under DWLS, your model only has to reproduce the estimated polychoric correlation matrix, not the actual observed response patterns.

> Or would you go for an MLR estimation that allows for robust standard errors?

If the latent normal item response assumption holds, then this would underestimate factor loadings (to degrees that depend on the distribution of thresholds), but structural parameters tend to be pretty unbiased either way.  Whether the chi-squared has inflated errors additionally depends on sample size.

http://psychmodels.ucdavis.edu/uploads/8/6/3/9/86398102/rhemtullabrosseauliardsavalei_pm.pdf

Either choice is based on dubious assumptions, so it just depends on which ones you are more comfortable putting your faith in.

https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2020.589965

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: Including missing with DWLS
messages.subject_clean: Including missing with DWLS
messages.body_plain:
> What is the difference between using missing="pairwise" with DWLS

This is a limited-information technique, and it assumes MCAR (restrictive, unrealistic).  For each pair of variables, it estimates their polychoric correlation using all available cases that provided data on both of those variables.

> vs. estimator="mml" and missing="fiml"?

This is a full-information technique, and it assumes MAR (less restrictive, realistic if your model includes variables related to missingness).  It is preferable in principle, but MML is very computationally intensive (requires numerical integration over the latent dimensions), so it may not be feasible for models with more than 2-3 latent variables.  Try running a single-factor CFA in lavaan to see how long that runs, then a 2-factor CFA and notice already how much that will increase the run time.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

Dear Mauricio,

I don't know how to explain this properly, but to me it seems like adding all the variables using ~~ at once is not the same as a "simple" correlation matrix. Maybe it is testing if not one but all variables correlate and therefore the results differ that much from the results that I get using manifest variables?
If I only add one of the variables to the strong boredom model as follows, the results match the ones I get using manifest variables:

bos5_0 ~ i5*1
bos6_0 ~ i6*1

bos5_1 ~~ bos5_2

boredom_2 ~ NA*1

boredom_2 ~~ NA*boredom_2

boredom_0 ~~ KC27pw_T

boredom_2 ~~ KC27pw_T
'

fit_strong_boredom_pw <- lavaan::cfa(strong_boredom_pw, data=df1, missing="FIML", estimator="MLR", std.lv <http://std.lv>=T)
summary(fit_strong_boredom_ph, fit.measures=T, standardized=T)

After running this model I would copied the code and only change the # correlation with KC27pw_T part to the next variable. This way my latent results match the manifest ones.

Strangely the covariances of the boredom time points are varying aroind +/- 0.001 between when I am running the models with only one variable one after another.

Manuel

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > You should use the function lavTestScore(weakmodel), these will do a LRT for each specific equality constraint in the model. So, you can identify if a single item may be problematic, if these is the case you can relase the equality constraint for only that 1 item. And if you are satisfied with that model, you can continue, this is called partial-measurement invariance. Its fine to continue if you have partial-invariance. The recommensation I make is to seek to have at least half the items being invariant to be able to make reliable inferences for latent parameters (like your growth curve). This comes from personla experience, I havent seen research suggesting a minimum threshold of items to be invariant

messages.body_plain:
Dear Terrence,

Thank you very much for your advice! And I am sorry that I am back for more support.

In the previous email, I asked about adjusted means of endogenous variables under the framework of SEM. You replied that in Step 8, the intercepts equality constraint should be the intercepts of endogenous common factors. I was wondering how it could be specified in lavaan?

> > 8. loadings + intercepts + regressions
> As long as you mean indicator intercepts in Step 2 and intercepts of endogenous common factors in Step 8, then that looks fine to me.

I tried group.equal = c("loadings","intercepts","regressions","means"). The inclusion of "intercepts" only constrained the exogenous latent variable indicators intercepts to be equal across groups. And the inclusion of "means" essentially made all the latent factors (exogenous and endogenous) to be zero across all the groups. Is there a way to formally specify exogenous common factor intercepts to be equal in lavaan? Or did I misunderstand?

Thank you very much for your support all along!

Kindly,
Erin

On Sat, 5 Dec 2020 at 02:43, Terrence Jorgensen <tjorge...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > 2. loadings + intercepts (scalar)
> > ...
> > 8. loadings + intercepts + regressions
>
> As long as you mean indicator intercepts in Step 2 and intercepts of endogenous common factors in Step 8, then that looks fine to me.
>
> Further, if Step 7's H0 is rejected, then you can also separately test lv.variances without constraining lv.covariances.  Possibly homoskedasticity holds but groups have unequal correlations.  Or possibly homoskedasticity holds for some factors but not others, in which case you can test equality of covariances among homoskedastic factors, but would need phantom constructs to test correlations among (homo- and) heteroskedastic factors.
>
> > More to step 8, I noticed that (for the non-reference groups) the unstandardised latent variable intercepts of exogenous variables shown in the summary output are the same as lavInspect (fit.model, "mean.lv <http://mean.lv>"). However, for endogenous latent variables as well as mediating latent variables, the intercepts shown are different between the summary output and "mean.lv <http://mean.lv>". Is it because one is the unadjusted mean ("mean.lv <http://mean.lv>" approach, not controlled for predictors) and the other is the adjusted mean (summary output, controlled for predictors)?
>
> Correct, "mean.lv <http://mean.lv>" returns model-implied latent-variable grand means, not the intercepts (the latter of which are the model parameters).
>
> A variable's intercept is always interpreted as its expected value when its predictor(s) == 0, so an intercept is only an "adjusted mean" (as the term is used in texts about ANCOVA) if the predictors' GRAND means happen to be zero (i.e., in all groups).  Likewise, variable's intercept is its grand mean (in any particular group) only when the variable has no predictor(s) OR its predictors' means all == 0 (in that group).
>
> > For categorical indicators -- objective: compare latent means for one measurement model (one latent factor with both binary and polytomous indicators):
>
> How many categories does the polytomous indicators have?  If only 3, then your sequence below is fine, but your configural model can already constrain thresholds to equality (it is statistically equivalent to equating the intercepts and latent scales, which is the default).
>
> > Using the Wu and Estabrook (2016) approach and measEq.syntax function to generate correct lavaan model syntax (parameterization = "delta" ):
> > 1. configural model: (ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>", ID.cat="Wu", group.equal="configural")
>
> Don't set group.equal= to anything if you are constraining anything.  "configural" is not a type of parameter.
>
> > 2. metric model:  (ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>", ID.cat="Wu", group.equal=c("thresholds","loadings")) -- this model constrains intercept as zero for the reference group and free the other groups.
>
> If your polytomous indicators have > 3 categories, you can separately test equality of thresholds first, then additionally constrain loadings (of items whose thresholds are invariant).  But other than being more informative about the type of DIF, I don't think there is a practical advantage to knowing whether there is DIF in thresholds vs loadings.  But the latter are only comparable when thresholds are equal.
>
> > 3. scalar model: (ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>", ID.cat="Wu", group.equal=c("thresholds","loadings","intercepts")) -- this model essentially constrains intercepts as zero for all groups.
> > If the scalar model holds, it is possible to compare latent means across groups.
>
> Yes, although partial scalar invariance is also sufficient.
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
>

> --

So, you can identify if a single item may be problematic, if these is the case you can relase the equality constraint for only that 1 item. And if you are satisfied with that model, you can continue, this is called partial-measurement invariance. Its fine to continue if you have partial-invariance. The recommensation I make is to seek to have at least half the items being invariant to be able to make reliable inferences for latent parameters (like your growth curve). Regressions with factor scores will be bias, unless you do some method to account for correction, like Croon's bias correction, or plausible values. Just adding your estimated factor scores into your data set will give you bias regressions.

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > You should use the function lavTestScore(weakmodel), these will do a LRT for each specific equality constraint in the model. So, you can identify if a single item may be problematic, if these is the case you can relase the equality constraint for only that 1 item. And if you are satisfied with that model, you can continue, this is called partial-measurement invariance. Its fine to continue if you have partial-invariance. The recommensation I make is to seek to have at least half the items being invariant to be able to make reliable inferences for latent parameters (like your growth curve). This comes from personla experience, I havent seen research suggesting a minimum threshold of items to be invariant

Regressions with factor scores will be bias, unless you do some method to account for correction, like Croon's bias correction, or plausible values. Just adding your estimated factor scores into your data set will give you bias regressions.

So, you can identify if a single item may be problematic, if these is the case you can relase the equality constraint for only that 1 item. And if you are satisfied with that model, you can continue, this is called partial-measurement invariance. Its fine to continue if you have partial-invariance. The recommensation I make is to seek to have at least half the items being invariant to be able to make reliable inferences for latent parameters (like your growth curve). This comes from personla experience, I havent seen research suggesting a minimum threshold of items to be invariant

messages.body_plain:
> Is there a way to add Bonferroni correction to the p-values?

You could just use an adjusted alpha level.  Or to adjust p values, you can use the p.adjust() function.  To access the vector of p values, use parameterEstimates()

PE <- parameterEstimates(fit_strong_boredom_correlation)
PE$p.bonf <- p.adjust(PE$pvalue, method = "bonferroni")

> Since all of them are 0.000 and options(digits=10) does not work

Use the nd= argument to lavaan's summary() method

summary(fit_strong_boredom_correlation, fit.measures=T, standardized=T, nd = 6)

messages.subject: Re: Testing measurement/structural invariance
messages.subject_clean: Testing measurement/structural invariance
messages.body_plain:
> intercepts of endogenous common factors. I was wondering how it could be specified in lavaan?

>  ...

> I tried group.equal = c("loadings","intercepts","regressions","means").

That should do it.
"loadings" refers to loadings of observed indicators on latent common factors (i.e., the lambda matrix)
"intercepts" refers to intercepts of observed indicators (or their latent item responses, if the observations are ordered= categorical), i.e., the vector "nu"
"regressions" refers to any effects of a latent common factor on another latent common factor (i.e., the "beta" matrix), which therefore includes higher-order loadings
"means" refers to intercepts of latent variables (both endogenous common-factor intercepts and exogenous common-factor means), i.e., the vector "alpha"

Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Re: Encountering a problem in LAVAAN - second-order factor
messages.subject_clean: Encountering a problem in LAVAAN - second-order factor
messages.body_plain:
> Yes, I used <reliabilityL2> for my 2nd order factor (IC). However, reliability is treating everything but KI, KEX, and CK as 2nd order factors.

Interesting, my check for higher-order factors removed exogenous latent factors, which of course (incorrectly) assumes all first-order factors are endogenous indicators of higher-order factors.  I don't know of a good solution for this.  The original check simply looked for patterns of (non)zero loadings in the lambda and beta matrices, but that cause problems when people wanted reliability using models with different latent structures.  For example, you could have a higher-order factor with a mix of both latent and observed indicators.

Now I am thinking that the best solution is to add a new argument, like higher= in reliabilityL2(), to name factors which should be omitted from the reliability calculation.  But it could be more general, like omit= to drop any factor whose composite reliability would not be of interest.

I'll work on that for the next version of semTools.  For now, you could simply remove the higher-order factor and fit a first-order CFA to pass to reliability().

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

I only learned that term when you posted it.  I am unfamiliar with how the weights are applied.  If the calculation of RDS weights allows them to be treated as normal sampling weights, then you can pass that variable name to lavaan's sampling.weights= argument.  If the "reference ID" variable indicates who knows whom in the snowball sampling, I doubt that can be treated as independent clusters using lavaan's cluster= argument because connections among individuals are more like an interpersonal network. messages.subject: Re: lavaan wih RDS
messages.subject_clean: lavaan wih RDS
messages.body_plain:
RDS has its own set of diagnostics of how much you can trust the statistical results -- roughly speaking, the recruitment chain must forget its initial (often very nonrandom) starting point, much like you'd have to burnin with MCMC. If all recruitment chains are of length 3, then the results are going to be crap no matter how hard you pretend they aren't.

As far as GEE models go, you can probably fake the spatial correlations by feeding the "neighbor" / connection matrices. Although frankly I don't know if that is properly supported by any R packages -- see if anything under "Spatial regression" under https://cran.rstudio.com/web/views/Spatial.html could work.

Terrence Jorgensen schrieb am Dienstag, 26. Januar 2021 um 19:46:51 UTC+1:
> > I had the (maybe stupid?) idea of using using lavCov() to create a polychoric covariance matrix that I then can use as an input for ML estimation
>
> You can't trust the SEs or test statistics because they treat the polychorics as known observations rather than as estimates (with their own SEs).  Taking the uncertainty of the first-step estimates into account is what DWLS does.
>
> > I was wondering what you would suggest as the best method?
>
> Depends how you define "best", and what your sample size is, and some other properties of the observed data, and some properties of the assumed latent responses if you use DWLS.
>
> > Can I ignore the warning, as estimation seems to be okay?
>
>  Probably, if there are no other signs of empirical underidentification.
>
> > Or is it sensible to use the polychoric covariance matrix, as this way the covariances that are used for estimation reflect the data better?
>
> You cannot compare fit across those estimators because they are based on different (assumptions about the) data.  Under DWLS, your model only has to reproduce the estimated polychoric correlation matrix, not the actual observed response patterns.
>
> > Or would you go for an MLR estimation that allows for robust standard errors?
>
> If the latent normal item response assumption holds, then this would underestimate factor loadings (to degrees that depend on the distribution of thresholds), but structural parameters tend to be pretty unbiased either way.  Whether the chi-squared has inflated errors additionally depends on sample size.
>
> http://psychmodels.ucdavis.edu/uploads/8/6/3/9/86398102/rhemtullabrosseauliardsavalei_pm.pdf
>
> Either choice is based on dubious assumptions, so it just depends on which ones you are more comfortable putting your faith in.
>
> https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2020.589965
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Estimating Bifactor Indices (PUC, ECV, H, FD) with ordered categorical indicators (using WLSMV or ULSMV)
messages.subject_clean: Estimating Bifactor Indices (PUC, ECV, H, FD) with ordered categorical indicators (using WLSMV or ULSMV)
messages.body_plain:
Hi

Shorter story: I'm calculating PUC, ECV, H, and FD for a bifactor model following  Rodriguez, Reise, and Haviland (2016). Would the equations need changes to work with ordered categorical indicators (using WLSMV or ULSMV)?  Rodriguez et al. exemplify with a Likert scale but only work with the polychoric correlation marix. The calculations I'm currently using for continuous outcomes (using MLR) or non mean/variance adjusted DWLS are at the end.

Btw, of course I'm not aware of these indices being included in any lavaan-related package (e.g. semTools). I hope I did not miss that. In any case, would you consider that useful or feasible in the future?

Longer story:

I am analyzing a bifactor model with ordered categorical outcomes (5 points Likert-type scale). Following  Rodriguez, Reise, and Haviland (2016) I am studying  (1) the reliability of unit-weighted composite scores; (2) the use of a set of items to compute factor scores or to identify a latent variable in an SEM context; and (3) whether multidimensional (bifactor) data are “unidimensional enough” to specify a unidimensional measurement model in an SEM context.

The first aspect is dealt with omega hierarchical which as far as I know is adapted for categorical indices in `semTools::reliability` following different equations from Green and Yang (2009).

For the second aspect, Rodriguez et al. recommend using indices H and FD. For the third, they advise calculating explained common variance of the general factor on all items (ECV) and on specific items (I-ECV), as well as the percentage of uncontaminated correlations (PUC). Except for PUC, I am not sure if the formulas they propose are directly applicable when working with ordered categorical indicators using mean and variance adjusted estimators (WLSMV/ULSMV).

I'm sorry if the answers are obvious and in the case of  PUC I honestly can't imagine how it would be different. I try my best to understand rigorously what I do, but due to my still limited knowledge on the mathematics underlying WLSMV (or ULSMV), I preferred to ask here since most members will know better.

Many thanks in advance
Manuel

References

Rodriguez A, Reise SP, Haviland MG. Evaluating bifactor models: calculating and interpreting statistical indices. Psychol Methods. 2016;21(2):137.

Code

These are the formulas I've used when treating the indicators as continuous (MLR) taken initially from  https://github.com/ddueber/BifactorIndicesCalculator :

fit <- cfa(model = bifactor.model, data = data, estimator = "WLSMV")

fit.std <- lavInspect(fit, "std")

Lambda <- fit.std$lambda
Lambda[is.na <http://is.na>(Lambda)] <- 0
Lambda <- as.matrix(Lambda)

Theta <- fit.std$theta
Phi <- fit.std$psi
class(Phi) <- "matrix"

#######
# ECV #
#######

# Rodriguez et al. (2016, equation 10)

ECV_SS_C <- function(Fac, Lambda) {
      inFactor <- Lambda[, Fac] != 0
      L2 = Lambda^2
      sum(L2[, Fac] * inFactor)/sum(L2 * inFactor)
}
ECV_results <- sapply(1:ncol(Lambda), ECV_SS_C, Lambda)
names(ECV_results) <- colnames(Lambda)
ECV_results

#######
# PUC #
#######

# Rodriguez et al. (2016, no equation but example in p. 144)

numItemsOnFactor <- colSums(Lambda != 0)
specificCorrelationCount <- sum(sapply(numItemsOnFactor,
                                       function(x) {
                                             x * (x - 1)/2
                                       })) - (nrow(Lambda) * (nrow(Lambda) - 1)/2)
1 - specificCorrelationCount/(nrow(Lambda) * (nrow(Lambda) -
                                                    1)/2)

#####
# H #
#####

# Rodriguez et al. (2016, equation 9)

1/(1 + 1/(colSums(Lambda ^2/(1 - Lambda^2))))

######
# FD #
######

# Rodriguez et al. (2016, equation 8)

Psi <- diag(Theta)
Sigma <- Lambda %*% Phi %*% t(Lambda) + diag(Psi)
FacDet <- sqrt(diag(Phi %*% t(Lambda) %*% solve(Sigma) %*%
                          Lambda %*% Phi))
names(FacDet) <- colnames(Lambda)
FacDet
